newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish National Assembly passes new constitution.
newsitem.headline: Polish National Assembly passes new constitution.

text.p: Poland's national assembly of both houses of parliament on Saturday passed a new constitution which replaces the obsolete 1952 communist era law eight years after the fall of communism in Poland.

The National Assembly voted 461 to 31 with five abstentions in favour of the new constitution which will now go to President Aleksander Kwasniewski, who is not expected to introduce any major changes.
"I announce that the National Assembly, with a majority of two thirds of votes, passed the constitution of the Republic of Poland," lower house speaker Jozef Zych told the assembly.
Deputies greeted the passing of the bill with a standing ovation and sang Poland's national anthem.
"This constitution, passed in fully democratic conditions ...stresses and protects citizen and human rights, as well as strengthens the state by boosting its executive powers," Zych said.
"It ensures the development of a market economy at the same time as guaranteeing the necessary level of social security of citizens," he added.
The president has 60 days to introduce amendments to the draft, but Kwasniewski, who was present during the vote, has already said he would not take longer than a few days.
The bill will then return to the National Assembly for a final reading and vote and will then be submitted to a national referendum, probably on May 25.

The new constitution guarantees free publicly-funded basic health care for all regardless of income and free education, although the draft admits the possibility of some charges for higher state education.
The presidency would be slightly weakened, with parliament allowed to overturn the president's veto with three-fifths of votes in the lower house rather than the present two-thirds majority.
The president would also have less say in appointments in the foreign, defence and interior ministries.
The draft states that "the Polish state guarantees legal protection of every man's life" but does not specify whether from the moment of conception or birth.
It enshrines equal rights for all churches and religious oragnisations and the state's impartiality towards all religious beliefs.
Poland's economic system is to be a "social market economy based on the freedom of economic enterprise, private property as well as solidarity, dialogue and the cooperation of social partners."

Deputies, who have worked on the draft for three years, were keen to pass the new charter before general elections due this autumn because a different government might order work on re-writing the constitution to start all over again.

According to the latest opinion polls, rightist parties supportive of the Catholic Church are likely to do well in parliamentary elections, replacing the legislature's current domination by ex-communists.
The rightist parties, mostly grouped around the Solidarity trade union, support their own draft constitution, in which the Christian idea of natural law takes precedence over codified laws.
